results.text: Somatic Experiencing can be useful early when activation is difficult to regulate. Rather than requiring a detailed trauma narrative, it focuses on sensation, orientation, impulses, defensive responses, and pacing so that activation can be noticed without becoming overwhelming. Titration, pendulation, and orientation are practical ways to expand the window of tolerance by approaching difficult material in manageable doses and then returning to a more regulated state. Capacity-building should not become indefinite, however. If someone is stable and has one clear target, they may already be ready for focused trauma work.

results.text: When activation runs away with you, Somatic Experiencing gives you something smaller to work with than the whole trauma story. You can stay with a sensation, an impulse, orientation, or a defensive response, with the pacing set by how much is actually manageable. Titration, pendulation, and orientation are different ways of touching something difficult in a small dose and then coming back. That is the practical side of the “window of tolerance” idea. If you can already do that and you have one clear target, you may be ready to work on the trauma itself; preparation should not become the treatment forever.
